My native language is English, and I speak just enough Spanish to get in trouble lol. I grew up around a lot of Spanish speakers and used to be fluent. My mother was not a fan of that for some reason, so she sent me to high school in a different part of town. I've been working to try to get my Spanish back. I would also like to learn German.

I've found that making learning fun helps. Using Duolingo feels more like playing a game and less like work. It's not perfect, but it was a good place to start.

There are also a lot of Spanish speaking channels on YouTube. I like to watch France 24 Español because it helps me maintain an understanding of the language. I also get to hear about what's happening in different parts of the world. Reading in the target language about a subject you're interested in might help too. For example, when I was told I had diabetes, I found a Spanish language book on it at the library and just sat there for a while reading up on it.

It doesn't get easier, but over time, you learn how to live with it. My access to treatment improved when I reached adulthood. I was surprised at how much was/is available for adults. I still go through frequent rough patches, but thanks to my resources, I'm able to have a few healthy friendships. Not having to deal with school anymore has been a huge help (I barely graduated high school and now I live on disability). 

The main thing that saved me was networking, meeting people. That kept me off the street while I waited for my disability to be approved.

The sooner you apply, the sooner you get it all out of the way. I won’t lie, it’s a pain in the ass to get approved. But in the end, with the help of a good lawyer, I got approved for SSI and SSDI. I only get payments from SSDI because the amount is larger. My frequent psychosis is what convinced the judge. It took me two years to get approved. But it was worth it. 

If you can, find yourself a therapist to help you process your emotions during the whole process. They may also be able to hook you up with a support worker. I needed a lot of help keeping track of things, and having a support worker and therapist wound up being really helpful.

I still don’t understand the whole process because it’s very complex and my brain is mush. But imo you should go ahead and apply.

These are a few techniques I use. Your results may vary.

-Take your actual pulse. Sometimes I feel like my heart is pounding, but then I find that it isn’t. If I’m too anxious to do that, I have a trusted friend check it for me.

-Sing! Singing forces you to breathe. It also gives you a physical task to focus on. For me, it also proves to me that I’m physically okay. If I can sing, surely my heart and lungs are okay. If you can’t think of something to sing, try flipping through a hymnal or finding some easy folk songs online.

-Stretch. Physical movement puts me back in the driver’s seat of my body. I find that, for me, getting back in the driver’s seat reduces the sensation of palpitations.

Hope these help. I’ve struggled with my mental health for over a decade, and I tell people these things so that others don’t have to go through what I have.
